summary: Defines a MIB module for managing MAC bridges based on IEEE 802.1D-1998 between LAN segments. It supports transparent bridging and covers other bridging types. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A bridge connects two parts of a local network. This memo defines the dials and readouts a manager uses to look after such a bridge.

questions: how to monitor spanning tree with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP object definitions that let a manager read and configure an Ethernet-style bridge and its spanning tree.

tldr.problem: Bridges connect LAN segments below the network layer, but network managers had no standard way to inspect or configure them over SNMP in the newer SMIv2 syntax.
tldr.mechanism: The BRIDGE-MIB module defines managed objects in subtrees for generic bridge and port data, the Spanning Tree Protocol, transparent bridging and static address filtering, based on IEEE 802.1D-1998.
tldr.outcome: It is a translation of the RFC 1493 module to SMIv2 with a few additions, and it obsoletes RFC 1493.

today: RFC 4188 is a Proposed Standard and the status metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1493.

sections.title: What the Bridge MIB Covers
sections.content:
A bridge connects Local Area Network (LAN) segments below the network layer. RFC 4188 defines the objects for managing such a device, based on the IEEE 802.1D-1998 standard. Two bridging modes exist, transparent and source route. This memo covers objects for a bridge in the transparent mode, plus some objects that apply to all types of bridges.

The module is a translation of the BRIDGE-MIB from RFC 1493 into SMIv2 syntax, and it obsoletes that RFC. As with other MIB modules, the objects are reached through SNMP and described with the Structure of Management Information (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.eli5: A bridge is like a doorway between two rooms. This document lists all the gauges and switches a grown-up can use to watch and adjust that doorway.

sections.title: Design Goals and Module Structure
sections.content:
The authors tried to keep the module as simple as possible. Objects had to meet criteria such as: start with a small set of essential objects, be essential for fault or configuration management, show evidence of current use, and not be derivable from other objects. They also avoided heavy instrumentation, following a guideline of one counter per critical section per layer.

Objects sit under dot1dBridge in five subtrees:

  • dot1dBase: objects for all types of bridges.
  • dot1dStp: Spanning Tree Protocol state; not implemented if the node does not run the protocol.
  • dot1dSr: source route bridging, described in RFC 1525.
  • dot1dTp: transparent bridging; not implemented if transparent bridging is unsupported.
  • dot1dStatic: destination-address filtering; not implemented if that is unsupported.

Where an IEEE 802.1D management object overlaps with an existing MIB object, it is left out. For example, Bridge.BridgeName is the same as sysDescr and BridgePort.PortName is the same as ifDescr.
sections.eli5: The makers wanted a short checklist, not a giant one. They only kept gauges that someone really needs, and sorted them into five labelled drawers.

sections.title: Bridge Ports and Interfaces
sections.content:
The dot1dBase subtree holds the bridge address (dot1dBaseBridgeAddress), the number of ports (dot1dBaseNumPorts) and the bridge type (dot1dBaseType), which is one of unknown, transparent-only, sourceroute-only or srt. A table with one row per port adds the port number, the matching interface index, a circuit identifier and two discard counters: frames dropped for excessive transit delay and for excessive size.

Each bridge port is tied to one interface in the IF-MIB, though several ports can share one interface (the RFC's example is several X.25 virtual circuits on one interface). A port number has no mandatory relationship to an interface number, and port numbers run from 1 to dot1dBaseNumPorts. The counters only cover traffic of protocols that are actually being bridged.

The module also expects the SNMPv2-MIB objects sysDescr and sysUpTime and the IF-MIB objects ifIndex, ifType, ifDescr, ifPhysAddress and ifLastChange to be implemented for full coverage of the 802.1D management objects.
sections.eli5: Each plug on the bridge is a port with a number. The bridge keeps a tally of how many messages it threw away because they were too slow or too big.

sections.title: Spanning Tree State and Timers
sections.content:
The optional dot1dStp subtree is for bridges that run the Spanning Tree Protocol. At the bridge level it reports the protocol version in use, the bridge priority, the designated root, the root cost, the root port, topology change counts and the timers MaxAge, HelloTime, HoldTime and ForwardDelay. The writable bridge-level values dot1dStpBridgeMaxAge, dot1dStpBridgeHelloTime and dot1dStpBridgeForwardDelay are what all bridges use when this bridge is the root.

A per-port table reports each port's priority, state, enable flag, path cost, and the designated root, cost, bridge and port for its segment. Port state is one of disabled, blocking, listening, learning, forwarding or broken. A port the bridge finds malfunctioning is placed in broken.

Timers are in hundredths of a second in this MIB, but in 1/256 second units inside a BPDU. The Timeout textual convention gives conversion formulas and says to multiply first, then divide. dot1dStpPortPathCost32 was added for IEEE 802.1t; the older 16-bit dot1dStpPortPathCost reports its maximum value, 65535, when the real cost does not fit.
sections.eli5: Bridges in a loop could pass messages round and round forever. The spanning tree is a rule book that switches off some paths so there is one clear route, and these gauges show which path each plug is using.

sections.title: Forwarding Database and Static Filters
sections.content:
The dot1dTp subtree is for transparent bridging. It counts Forwarding Database entries discarded because of lack of storage (dot1dTpLearnedEntryDiscards) and sets the aging time for dynamically learned entries (dot1dTpAgingTime, 10 to 1000000 seconds, with 300 seconds recommended by 802.1D-1998). The forwarding table lists each unicast MAC address, the port it was seen on, and a status of other, invalid, learned, self or mgmt. A port table adds the maximum INFO field size and counters for frames in, frames out and frames filtered.

The optional dot1dStatic subtree holds filtering rules set by management. Each entry is keyed by a destination address and a receive port, where port 0 means all ports without a more specific entry. dot1dStaticAllowedToGoTo is a bit string with one bit per port, first octet covering ports 1 through 8. Its value may exceed the 484-byte minimum SNMP message size over UDP, so engines on bridges with many ports must support suitable message sizes. Status values are other, invalid, permanent, deleteOnReset and deleteOnTimeout.
sections.eli5: A bridge learns which kid lives behind which door by watching who sends notes. It remembers this for a while, and a grown-up can also write fixed rules about who may pass which door.

sections.title: Notifications and Conformance
sections.content:
Two optional notifications are defined. newRoot says the sending agent has become the new root of the spanning tree. topologyChange is sent when a configured port moves from Learning to Forwarding or from Forwarding to Blocking, and it is not sent if a newRoot notification is sent for the same transition.

The module also defines groups and two compliance statements. The older bridgeCompliance1493 matches RFC 1493, and bridgeCompliance4188 is the new one. Under the first, the base groups are mandatory for every bridge. The spanning tree groups are mandatory for bridges that support the Spanning Tree Protocol, and the transparent bridging groups are mandatory for bridges supporting transparent mode. The static filtering and notification groups are optional.
sections.eli5: The bridge can ring a bell when it becomes the boss of the network or when a door opens or closes. Which gauges a bridge must have depends on what jobs it does.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects can hurt if left unprotected. Unauthorized writes to the spanning tree objects can make the protocol compute other default topologies or change how quickly it reacts to failures. Setting dot1dTpAgingTime to a large value may simplify forwarding table overflow attacks. Write access to the static table can turn off provisioned filtering or add filters that block rightful use of the network.

Readable data is sensitive too. The tables reveal topology and active stations, and the addresses in the forwarding table usually reveal the manufacturer of the MAC hardware. Forged newRoot and topologyChange notifications could cause a management system to do needless work, which may be part of a denial of service attack.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and it RECOMMENDS that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can turn the dials on your bridge, they can make your network slow or block people. So only trusted people should be allowed to read or change them.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1493
sections.content:
The main change is the translation of the definitions to SMIv2, including conformance statements, textual conventions and UNITS clauses. Other changes:

  • dot1dStpPortPathCost32 was added to support IEEE 802.1t.
  • Permitted values of dot1dStpPriority and dot1dStpPortPriority were clarified for bridges supporting IEEE 802.1t or 802.1w.
  • The meaning of dot1dStpTimeSinceTopologyChange was clarified for bridges supporting the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol.
  • Boilerplate, security text and references were updated.
sections.eli5: This is a tidied-up copy of an older rule sheet, with a bigger counter for fast links and a few unclear lines fixed.
